questions.q: According to the episode, which elements did Big Bang nucleosynthesis actually produce in the first ~20 minutes of the universe?
options: Hydrogen, helium and a barest trace of lithium
Hydrogen, helium, carbon and oxygen
All elements up to iron
Only hydrogen
questions.explanation: The fusion window slammed shut after about 20 minutes, leaving the universe roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass with a sprinkle of lithium. Everything heavier — carbon, oxygen, iron, gold — had to be built later, inside stars.

questions.q: What is the net result of the proton-proton chain in a star like the Sun?
options: Two protons fuse into a single deuterium nucleus, releasing no energy
Four protons are fused into one helium-4 nucleus, releasing about 26.7 MeV
Helium is split back into four protons, absorbing energy
Carbon is fused into oxygen, releasing about 7.65 MeV
questions.explanation: Four protons go in and one helium-4 nucleus comes out. The helium weighs about 0.7% less than the four protons, and by E = mc² that vanished mass reappears as roughly 26.7 MeV of energy per completed chain.

questions.q: In the CNO cycle, what role do the carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nuclei play?
options: They are the fuel that is consumed to make energy
They are the final products built up from hydrogen
They act as catalysts — borrowed and returned, so the carbon-12 is handed back at the end
They are waste products that poison the reaction
questions.explanation: The carbon is borrowed and returned, like tongs used to handle hot coals — it is not used up. The net result is identical to the proton-proton chain: four protons in, one helium-4 out, about 26.7 MeV released. Calling C, N and O the products is the classic error.

questions.q: Why does the proton-proton chain dominate in the Sun while the CNO cycle takes over in hot, massive stars?
options: The CNO cycle only works where there is no carbon present
The CNO cycle is far more sensitive to temperature (roughly T¹⁷ versus T⁴ for the pp chain), so it roars into life only at high core temperatures
The proton-proton chain releases far more energy per reaction
Massive stars have cooler cores than the Sun
questions.explanation: The pp chain ramps up gently, roughly as the fourth power of temperature; the CNO cycle climbs as about the seventeenth power. So in the cool Sun the pp chain does over 98% of the work, but in hot, massive stars the savage CNO cycle dominates completely.

questions.q: What was Fred Hoyle's audacious 1953 prediction that made the triple-alpha process viable?
options: That beryllium-8 is perfectly stable and never decays
That carbon-12 has an undiscovered excited energy level (resonance) at about 7.65 MeV that hugely boosts carbon production
That iron-56 sits at the peak of the binding-energy curve
That neutron stars collide to make gold
questions.explanation: Reasoning backwards from the fact that the universe is full of carbon and that we exist, Hoyle predicted a resonance of carbon-12 near 7.65 MeV. The energy of a beryllium-8 plus a helium nucleus lands almost exactly on it, like a doorbell tuned to the right note, so carbon forms readily. The Kellogg lab team confirmed the 'Hoyle state'.

questions.q: Why does fusion in a massive star stop at iron — the 'iron wall'?
options: Iron is too rare for the star to find
Iron-56 sits at the peak of the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve (about 8.79 MeV per nucleon), so fusing iron costs energy rather than releasing it
Iron melts and drains out of the core
Iron absorbs all the neutrinos, halting the reaction
questions.explanation: Climbing the periodic table by fusion releases energy until iron, the most tightly bound nucleus the star can reach. Fusing iron into something heavier yields a less tightly bound product, so it costs energy — the fuel that held the star up against gravity stops working.

questions.q: Once the iron core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit (~1.4 solar masses), what happens, and how are elements heavier than iron made?
options: The core cools quietly into a white dwarf, and heavy elements form by slow fusion
Electron degeneracy pressure fails, the core collapses into neutron matter, and the supernova's neutron flood builds elements heavier than iron by neutron capture
The star simply stops shining with no further events
The iron fuses directly into gold and uranium, releasing energy
questions.explanation: Beyond ~1.4 solar masses electron degeneracy pressure can no longer hold; the core collapses to neutron matter in under a second and the star explodes as a supernova. In that storm of neutrons, nuclei capture neutron after neutron to build gold, lead and uranium — elements ordinary fusion can never make.

questions.q: From memory: explain the central tug-of-war that governs the entire life of a star, and what happens to it when the core fuel runs out.
keyPoints: A star is a balance between gravity pulling inward and the outward pressure from fusion energy pouring out of the core.
While fusion burns, the two forces are balanced and the star is stable (the main sequence).
When the core fuel runs out, fusion pressure drops, gravity wins, and the core collapses — heating up until it crosses the threshold to ignite the next fuel (e.g. helium at ~100 million K).
questions.explanation: If you recalled gravity-in versus fusion-pressure-out, and that collapse heats the core to ignite the next fuel, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: why did Fred Hoyle name the 'Big Bang', and what was ironic about his legacy?
keyPoints: On BBC radio in 1949 Hoyle used 'Big Bang' dismissively, to mock the rival theory that the universe began in one hot, dense moment.
Hoyle himself backed the steady-state theory (an eternal, unchanging universe) and fought the Big Bang to his death in 2001.
The irony: his steady-state theory is now dead, yet the insulting name he coined became the accepted model — while he was magnificently right about how stars forge the elements.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that the name was an insult from a steady-state advocate, and the irony that the name stuck while his cosmology was wrong, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: The Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second, and about 0.7% of that mass is converted directly into energy. How many tonnes of mass are turned into energy each second?
questions.given: Mass fused per second \(= 600 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{tonnes}\);  fraction converted \(= 0.7\% = 0.007\)
working: This matches the episode's figure of 'around four million tonnes' converted to pure energy each second.
questions.explanation: Multiplying the 600 million tonnes fused by the 0.7% mass deficit gives about 4.2 million tonnes of mass turned into energy every second, by E = mc².
